sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on governance structures and reporting lines: board and committee charters, a schedule of AI briefings, management dashboards, and a documented AI use-case inventory. It depends on a regulatory change log, a litigation watchlist, an incident reporting channel, and a record of model provenance, validation, and monitoring. Legal and compliance teams supply the underlying evidence through contracts, data maps, impact assessments, audit findings, and board minutes. Many organizations use governance, risk and compliance platforms, board portals, and AI registries to keep that evidence current and retrievable. The infrastructure is less about a single tool and more about a repeatable cycle of inquiry, documentation, and follow-up.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method is disciplined inquiry: directors ask management how AI is used, what data trains it, how outputs are tested, who owns the risk, and what happens when something goes wrong. Advisors prepare briefing memos, risk heat maps, scenario analyses, and tabletop exercises that let the board test its oversight against plausible harms. The board then documents its questions, its reliance on management and experts, and its decisions, because process is often the central issue in oversight disputes. Committees review AI-related metrics, third-party contracts, incident reports, and remediation plans, and they escalate material matters to the full board. The work also includes director education, peer benchmarking, and periodic review of whether the board has the right expertise and information flow.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on fiduciary duties, disclosure obligations, intellectual property, privacy, and data provenance. With 92 of 149 active AI lawsuits being intellectual property matters, boards face direct questions about the provenance of training data, the rights attached to model outputs, and the terms of vendor and open source licenses. The 29 AI case law precedents and 222 compliance and regulation pages tracked by the site show that oversight standards and regulatory expectations are still forming. Boards also manage conflicts of interest, insider trading risk, indemnification, D&O insurance, privilege, and the risk of derivative claims. Provenance work includes documenting data sources, consent, licensing, model lineage, and the chain of custody for AI-generated records, because that evidence supports both defense and disclosure.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more explicit board ownership of AI risk, with dedicated AI committees, AI expertise on boards, and regular reporting on model performance, incidents, and regulatory change. As the count of state AI bills and active lawsuits grows, boards will likely see more shareholder proposals, disclosure demands, and oversight claims tied to AI. Assurance is moving from ad hoc review toward independent validation, provenance tracking, and audit trails that can be examined after the fact. Insurance markets, director education, and peer benchmarking will continue to adapt as courts and regulators clarify expectations. The practical effect is that board advisory work will become more continuous, more evidence-based, and more closely tied to the same data governance and compliance systems that manage AI day to day.
